We also explore the complete market pressures, from stretched valuations and rising volatility to leverage and changing investor sentiment and politics.

Global · Markets
US Midterm Results Trigger a Major Selloff in AI and Technology Stocks
The Democrats’ victory in the US midterm elections has brought renewed attention to the political and regulatory risks surrounding AI infrastructure. Their growing influence in Congress could increase scrutiny of the rapid expansion of data centres and the spending plans of major technology companies.
Three areas are particularly important for investors:
  • Data-centre expansion: Concerns around electricity bills, water consumption and pressure on local power grids could lead to tighter permitting requirements, greater scrutiny and project delays.
  • AI regulation: Democrats may push for stricter rules covering data privacy, consumer protection, transparency and corporate accountability.
  • Big Tech spending: The scale of AI infrastructure investment could face greater scrutiny, particularly around its impact on employment and whether the expected returns justify the expenditure.
Veto Stands Between Policy Changes
President Trump can veto legislation passed by Congress. Overriding that veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
A nationwide legislative restriction on AI infrastructure faces significant hurdles. However, congressional oversight, regulatory scrutiny and local permitting decisions could still increase costs and delay data-centre projects.
From Wall Street to Asian Technology Markets
The political shift added to existing concerns around stretched valuations, AI capital expenditure and crowded positioning, triggering a sharp selloff across global equity markets.
US markets - November 5
  • Nasdaq 100 fell more than 6%, its steepest decline since March 2020.
  • S&P 500 dropped 4.4%, while all 30 Dow constituents ended lower.
  • Russell 2000 declined 4.5%, indicating that selling extended beyond large-cap technology.
  • The Nasdaq 100 lost approximately $2.3 trillion in market value and stood nearly 15% below its October 6 record.
  • The semiconductor index (SOX) fell 12%, its worst session since March 2020, and was more than 38% below its June peak.
Global and thematic impact
The Asian market figures reflect November 6 trading, while US market figures reflect November 5.
The selloff was not limited to AI stocks. Momentum, semiconductor and heavily shorted strategies also came under pressure, suggesting that crowded positioning and risk reduction played a significant role.
Industry Reaction: CEOs and Investors Speak Out
The selloff has brought the political and economic challenges of AI infrastructure expansion into sharper focus. Meta’s Dina Powell McCormick: Warned that building data centres in the US could become more difficult. OpenAI’s Sam Altman: Emphasised that people should remain in control of AI. OpenAI also outlined commitments around power, infrastructure and community engagement. Elon Musk: Commented that “Data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now.” AMD’s Lisa Su: Highlighted the importance of ensuring that everyone benefits from AI. Jefferies’ Jane Gibbons: Described the market reaction as reactionary rather than a fundamental reset. Interactive Brokers’ Steve Sosnick: Cautioned that the underlying concerns driving the selloff cannot simply disappear. Technology companies may increasingly need to demonstrate how they will manage power requirements, infrastructure costs and community concerns. The ability to execute AI investment plans could become as important as the scale of spending itself.
Market Stress: Volatility, Leverage and Forced Selling
The scale of the decline was amplified by crowded positions, leverage and institutional risk reduction.
Market volatility surged as the VIX rose 11.57 points to 28.18, its highest level since March. Technology-focused long-short hedge funds lost more than 4% on Thursday as crowded positions came under pressure. Meanwhile, Nomura estimated that leveraged and inverse ETFs could generate approximately $47 billion in equity selling into Thursday’s close as they rebalance their exposure. Goldman Sachs also reported losses across fundamental long-short and multi-strategy hedge funds, while some managers began reducing risk. When leveraged positions and crowded trades unwind simultaneously, selling can become self-reinforcing. This can push prices below levels justified by changes in company fundamentals alone, although the extent of further forced selling remains uncertain.
What Does the Future Hold?
The AI investment cycle may become more selective as investors demand clearer evidence of returns on capital expenditure. Higher infrastructure costs, regulatory scrutiny and delays in project approvals could affect the pace and location of future data-centre expansion. However, this does not necessarily mean the AI investment cycle is over. Companies with strong balance sheets, existing computing capacity and demonstrable AI revenues may remain better positioned. Market instability is likely to persist until these new developments gain clarity and investor sentiment stabilises.
Why It Matters
Investors have become increasingly bullish on AI, with valuations and expectations built around sustained growth in AI spending. However, this selloff could bring investors back to reality by questioning whether massive capital expenditure can translate into sustainable returns. Regulatory scrutiny, infrastructure constraints and rising costs could challenge these expectations, putting pressure on valuations and exposing companies with weaker fundamentals.
